description:
MARINT is a maritime intelligence project focused on detecting suspicious and “dark” vessels using SAR satellite imagery, AIS data, radar information, and AI-based analysis.
Our goal is to create a clear operational picture that helps maritime authorities detect hidden activity, understand vessel behavior, and respond faster.
summary:
MARINT is an interactive web application that turns satellite radar (SAR) data into a live picture of what is happening above undersea cables and pipelines. It combines Sentinel-1 SAR imagery served by NASA (OPERA RTC-S1 through NASA GIBS, with pass times from NASA CMR) with live AIS ship positions, open infrastructure maps and public sanctions lists.

The change we track is at the sea surface: ships appearing, slowing, stopping, or going silent above critical infrastructure. MARINT detects ships directly in the radar image, compares them with AIS at the moment of the satellite pass, and flags targets that are not transmitting. It also scores vessel behaviour with transparent rules, such as the anchor-drag pattern behind recent cable damage in the Baltic Sea.

Every alert comes with its evidence: the track, the radar image, the rule that fired and a printable report. We use the Baltic Sea as our live example because all the needed data there is open. Our prototype uses Sentinel-1 SAR; the same method applies to NISAR data as it becomes available.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

MARINT is a browser-based console for monitoring ships around undersea cables and pipelines. Live demo: https://marint-baltic.vercel.app/

- Shows every AIS-transmitting vessel in the Gulf of Finland, refreshed every 60 seconds.

- Draws watch corridors around pipelines and cables and scores each vessel inside them from 0 to 100.

- Loads Sentinel-1 SAR imagery from NASA GIBS, detects ships in the image, and matches them to AIS positions at the satellite pass time. Unmatched targets are marked as possible dark vessels.

- Highlights vessels on public sanctions and shadow-fleet lists.

- Opens an investigation page for any vessel, with an evidence timeline, a radar image of its position, an assessment and a printable report.

- Saves a situation as a case file that can be replayed later.

HOW IT WORKS

Alerts come from transparent rules, each with a visible weight: stopped inside a corridor, a sharp speed drop while heading and course disagree (the anchor-drag signature), an AIS gap, long dwell time, vessel type and sanctions status. Strong wind lowers the score. Radar ship detection uses classical image processing: bright clusters well above the sea background, with fixed objects removed by comparing against an earlier image.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Since 2023, cables and pipelines in the Baltic have been damaged several times by ships dragging anchors, usually noticed only after the damage. MARINT is designed to flag that behaviour while it is happening, and to give the operator the reasons and the evidence, not just a score. It uses only open data and needs no API keys, so any maritime authority can try it immediately.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, MapLibre GL for the map, hosted on Vercel. No backend and no build step. Code was written with an AI coding assistant (Claude) under the team's direction.

CREATIVITY

We treat SAR as a change detector for human activity at sea, and fuse it with AIS in the browser, with no server.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Explainability over black-box scores; honesty about limits (some cable routes are approximate and are scored more cautiously; satellite passes are near-daily, not continuous); and that an alert is a prompt for human review, not proof of wrongdoing. The MVP is rule-based; a trained SAR detection model is the next step.

NEXT STEPS

Having successfully tested our approach with open NASA and Sentinel-1 imagery, we aim to overcome revisit delays through commercial contracts with Capella Space and Umbra (SAR), supported by BlackSky and Planet (optical). Our target is access to approximately 20 satellites (12 SAR and 8 optical), purchasing imaging services rather than satellites. By combining scheduled and on-demand imaging, we aim to reduce the revisit interval to as little as 15 minutes in priority maritime areas, enabling near-continuous monitoring of critical underwater infrastructure.
